title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: Cabbage Patch Kids: Must-Have Toy of the Century
summary: Josh and Chuck cover Cabbage Patch Kids as part of the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist. They trace the doll's origins from Xavier Roberts's 1977 "Little People" soft-sculpture dolls (needle molding, Appalachian origin myth, Babyland General in Cleveland, Georgia) to the 1982 Coleco partnership, the 1983 Christmas frenzy (Newsweek cover, store riots, Milwaukee DJ stunt), the 1984 resurgence, later owners and declines, and the Martha Nelson Thomas copyright lawsuit that Roberts settled in 1985. They also discuss the Garbage Pail Kids parody, and close with listener mail about beavers (Bev the beaver).

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Cabbage Patch Kids episode for the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist and shares a personal anecdote about his own doll. Chuck and Josh banter about their childhood dolls and the show's repeated coverage of the topic.

segments.title: What Cabbage Patch Kids are and their 1983 craze
segments.summary: The hosts explain what Cabbage Patch Kids were and how they became a huge Christmas 1983 craze. They cite a 1986 journal description of the dolls and a rumored, unproven claim that Ronald Reagan had a hand in the design.

segments.title: Xavier Roberts's origin myth and needle molding
segments.summary: Josh recounts the official Cabbage Patch Kids origin story from the company website involving bunny bees, a waterfall, and a cabbage patch. The hosts then give the more realistic account: Xavier Roberts studied art at Truett-McConnell and learned German needle molding technique starting in 1977.

segments.title: Little People dolls and early sales at Unicoy State Park
segments.summary: Chuck describes Xavier Roberts's 1977 Little People soft-sculpture dolls, sold as adoptions for about forty dollars at craft shows and gift shops such as Unicoy State Park. Josh notes a first-place win at an art show in Florida and the founding of Original Appalachian Artworks, which opened Babyland General.

segments.title: Babyland General and the adoption experience
segments.summary: The hosts describe Babyland General as a former hospital where staff dressed as doctors and nurses presented dolls being born from cabbages. Chuck recounts his family's experience with a doll with an uneven hairline, and notes the premature-baby awareness angle.

segments.title: Partnership with Coleco and mass production
segments.summary: In 1982 Xavier Roberts partnered with Coleco to mass-produce the dolls. Coleco kept the name Little People for a time, machine-made vinyl heads, shrank the dolls to about sixteen inches, and offered varied ethnicities, skin tones, and features to preserve individuality.

segments.title: Name change, adoption fees, and press coverage
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why the name was changed to Cabbage Patch Kids and how the adoption fee of about thirty dollars, roughly seventy-eight dollars today, combined with Coleco's media reach to drive press. A December 1983 Newsweek cover featuring a Cabbage Patch Kid ran just before the holiday buying season.

segments.title: Supply shortages, riots, and nightly news stories
segments.summary: Coleco sold over three million dolls by the end of 1983 but could not keep up with demand. Stories described shoppers pushing and fighting, parents driving across state lines, and a Kansas City postal carrier flying to London. The hosts reference a Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania store manager tossing dolls into a crowd.

segments.title: Black market, the Milwaukee bomber stunt, and 1984 sales
segments.summary: Stores with coupons moved distribution to loading docks, and secondary and black markets marked up prices. Local Milwaukee DJs staged a fake B-26 bomber drop at the Brewers stadium that drew people in subzero wind chill. The dolls were again the must-have toy in 1984, with about two billion dollars in sales that year.

segments.title: Space shuttle doll, Olympics, and Challenger documentary tangent
segments.summary: Josh mentions Christopher Xavier, a Cabbage Patch doll that flew on a 1985 Space Shuttle mission, and a doll that became a 1992 US Olympic team mascot. The hosts briefly discuss a Challenger documentary and the film Enola Holmes.

segments.title: Coleco decline, later owners, and failed spinoff toys
segments.summary: Coleco went bankrupt in the 1980s and the license passed to Mattel, Hasbro, Toys R Us, and then Play Along. Failed spinoffs included a talking doll, a swimming doll, and Mattel's Snack Time doll, which was withdrawn for safety issues. Quality declined in the 1990s before Toys R Us restored cloth bodies for the 2003 twentieth anniversary.

segments.title: Cabbage Patch Kids' revival and population stat
segments.summary: Cabbage Patch Kids were revived around the 2003 anniversary, with nostalgia buyers returning. The hosts note that over thirty-two years about 130 million dolls were adopted, equal to a population of the tenth-largest country, with one born every 6.8 seconds.

segments.title: Martha Nelson Thomas and the Little Doll Babies lawsuit
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that folk artist Martha Nelson Thomas created Little Doll Babies using the same needle-molding technique in the 1970s. Roberts sold her dolls under an agreement, then marked them up and started his own line after a dispute. Thomas sued, mainly because she had not copyrighted her work, and the case settled in 1985 for an undisclosed sum.

segments.title: Garbage Pail Kids parody and Art Spiegelman
segments.summary: Topps released the Garbage Pail Kids trading cards in 1985 as a parody of Cabbage Patch Kids. Roberts complained, and the cards were changed enough to avoid a tie-in. Art Spiegelman, who later created Maus, was an art director on the cards.

segments.title: Listener mail: beavers and Bev the beaver
segments.summary: A listener writes about the beaver episode and the video of Bev the beaver dragging household items to dam a doorway. The hosts respond to the email and invite more mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives the show credits and directs listeners to the iHeartRadio app.
